result: Tamoxifen treatment in Pkd1 ecKO mice reduced PC-1 protein to ~66.7% of control levels in mesenteric arteries without altering other proteins (PC-2, SK3, IK, TRPV4, Piezo1, eNOS, GPR68), and PC-1 labeling was absent in endothelial cells.
evaluation: Claims C1-C3 are supported by Western blot quantification (C1, C2) and immunofluorescence imaging (C3) shown in Figure 1A-C. The reduction to 66.7% is expected given that smooth muscle cells also express PC-1, and the specificity of PC-1 knockout to endothelial cells is confirmed by en face imaging. The lack of change in other proteins demonstrates specificity of the knockout.

result: Flow stimulates a PC-1-dependent biphasic current response in endothelial cells: an initial transient inward current (~-1.3 pA/pF) followed by a sustained Ca2+-dependent reduction in inward current (~-0.97 pA/pF). Both components are substantially reduced in Pkd1 ecKO cells (to 15.4% and 42.2% of control, respectively).
evaluation: Claims C4-C9 are well-supported by patch-clamp electrophysiology data in Figure 1D-F. The biphasic response is clearly demonstrated, and the Ca2+-dependence of the sustained component is shown by Ca2+ removal experiments. The substantial reduction in both components in Pkd1 ecKO cells (C6-C8) provides strong evidence for PC-1 dependence. Sample sizes appear adequate (n=15-16 cells).

result: PC-1 in endothelial cells contributes to flow-mediated arterial hyperpolarization. At 80 mmHg, intraluminal flow hyperpolarized Pkd1fl/fl arteries by ~10 mV but Pkd1 ecKO arteries by only ~2.6 mV (27.1% of control).
evaluation: Claims C10-C12 are supported by sharp microelectrode measurements in pressurized arteries (Figure 1G-H). The substantial reduction in flow-induced hyperpolarization in Pkd1 ecKO arteries provides strong evidence for PC-1's role. However, the authors acknowledge they did not verify cell types from which impalements were obtained, though they note ECs and smooth muscle cells are electrically coupled in resistance arteries.

result: PC-1 mediates flow-induced vasodilation over a broad shear stress range (3-35 dyn/cm²). Flow-mediated dilation in Pkd1 ecKO arteries was reduced to 34.8-50% of control, while ACh-induced vasodilation, myogenic tone, and other baseline parameters remained unchanged.
evaluation: Claims C13-C17 are supported by pressurized artery myography data (Figure 2A-D and supplements). The specificity of the effect to flow-mediated responses (not ACh) and the preservation of baseline vascular properties (C16) strengthen the conclusion that PC-1 specifically mediates flow sensing rather than causing general endothelial dysfunction. The broad shear stress range tested (C15) is a strength.

result: Flow-mediated PC-1-dependent vasodilation occurs via activation of eNOS, IK channels, and SK channels. PC-1 knockout reduced the L-NNA-, Tram-34-, and apamin-sensitive components to 21.6%, 13.5%, and 18.6% of control, respectively. Flow increased p-eNOS (S1176) 1.40-fold in control but not in Pkd1 ecKO arteries.
evaluation: Claims C18-C25 are supported by pharmacological inhibition experiments (Figure 2E-H) and Western blotting for eNOS phosphorylation (Figure 2I-J). The convergent evidence from multiple approaches (pharmacology and biochemistry) strengthens the conclusion. The specificity of phosphorylation changes (p-eNOS but not total eNOS) is appropriate. Sample sizes appear adequate.

result: EC-specific PC-1 knockout increases systemic blood pressure (MAP increased from ~89.9 to ~109.6 mmHg, 21.9% higher) without altering heart rate, activity, or kidney anatomy (proximal tubule diameter, glomerular surface area).
evaluation: Claims C26-C30 are supported by telemetric blood pressure measurements (Figure 3A-B) and histological analysis (Figure 3C-F). The preservation of kidney anatomy is important for ruling out renal cyst formation as a cause of hypertension. The experiments were performed single-blind, which is appropriate. However, the sample sizes are relatively small (n=5-7 mice), though power analysis was reportedly performed.

result: PC-1 and PC-2 coassemble and locate in close spatial proximity in endothelial cells. Co-immunoprecipitation confirmed physical association, and immunoFRET showed ~24.3% N-FRET in Pkd1fl/fl cells but only ~1.3% and 0.9% in Pkd1 ecKO and Pkd2 ecKO cells, respectively. Lattice-SIM imaging confirmed colocalization by Pearson's and Mander's coefficients.
evaluation: Claims C31-C35 are supported by multiple complementary techniques: co-IP (Figure 4A), immunoFRET (Figure 4B-C), and Lattice-SIM (Figure 4D-G). The convergent evidence from different imaging modalities strengthens the conclusion. The Förster coefficient of ~6.3 nm for the Alexa Fluor pair supports the close proximity interpretation. The dramatic reduction in FRET in knockout cells provides strong evidence for specificity.

result: PC-1 and PC-2 form discrete plasma membrane clusters in endothelial cells with similar densities. PC-1 clusters (mean ~3702.5 nm²) are larger than PC-2 clusters (mean ~2157.1 nm²). Approximately 27% of PC-1 clusters overlap with PC-2 clusters (vs. ~7.8% after randomization), with mean intercentroid distance of ~126.8 nm. Flow does not alter cluster properties.
evaluation: Claims C36-C44 are supported by SMLM-TIRF imaging with appropriate controls (Figure 5A-F). The localization precision (29.6±0.6 and 24.6±0.7 nm) is adequate for the measurements. The Costes' randomization analysis (C43) provides important statistical validation that the overlap is non-random. The exponential distribution of cluster sizes is appropriately characterized. The finding that flow doesn't alter cluster properties (C44) is important for the mechanistic model.

result: Knockout of either PC-1 or PC-2 abolishes surface expression of both proteins. In Pkd1 ecKO cells, PC-1 and PC-2 cluster densities were reduced to ~15.7% and 18.3% of control, cluster sizes to ~17.7% and 28.3%, intercentroid distance increased ~5.79-fold, and overlap reduced to ~1.2%. This demonstrates interdependency of PC-1 and PC-2 for surface trafficking.
evaluation: Claims C45-C51 are supported by SMLM-TIRF imaging comparing Pkd1fl/fl and Pkd1 ecKO cells (Figure 5A-F and supplements). The dramatic reductions in all cluster parameters in knockout cells provide strong evidence for interdependency. The interpretation that remaining fluorescence represents nonspecific secondary antibody labeling (C51) is reasonable given the minimal and random distribution. Similar results in Pkd2 ecKO cells (supplementary data) strengthen the conclusion.

result: Double knockout of PC-1 and PC-2 in endothelial cells (Pkd1/Pkd2 ecKO) reduced both proteins to ~60.9% and 66.1% of control without altering eNOS. Flow-mediated vasodilation was reduced to 38.8-50.4% of control at different shear stresses, while ACh responses, K+-induced constriction, myogenic tone, and passive diameter remained unchanged.
evaluation: Claims C52-C55 are supported by Western blotting (Figure 6A-B) and pressurized artery myography (Figure 6C-D and supplements). The double knockout provides important evidence that PC-1 and PC-2 function in the same pathway. The preservation of non-flow-mediated responses confirms specificity. The magnitude of inhibition is similar to single knockouts, supporting the interdependence model.

result: Flow stimulates sustained inward cation currents (ICat) of similar amplitude in Pkd1fl/fl and Pkd2fl/fl endothelial cells. Both PC-1 knockout and PC-2 knockout similarly reduce flow-activated ICat to ~23.3% and 22.5% of control, respectively, indicating PC-1 and PC-2 similarly contribute to flow-activated ICat.
evaluation: Claims C57-C60 are supported by patch-clamp electrophysiology using solutions to isolate cation currents (Figure 6E-G). The similar magnitude of reduction in both Pkd1 ecKO and Pkd2 ecKO cells provides strong evidence for interdependence. The experimental design appropriately isolates ICat by blocking K+ channels and removing Ca2+ from the bath. Sample sizes appear adequate (n=7-9 cells per condition).

result: Intracellular introduction of peptides corresponding to PC-1 or PC-2 coiled-coil domains similarly reduced flow-activated ICat to ~30.1% and 29% of control in both Pkd1fl/fl and Pkd2fl/fl cells, while scrambled peptides had no effect. This indicates PC-1 and PC-2 are interdependent and that physical coupling of their C-termini is necessary for flow activation.
evaluation: Claims C61-C64 are supported by patch-clamp experiments with interference peptides (Figure 6F-G and supplement). The similar effects of PC-1 and PC-2 coiled-coil peptides in both genotypes, combined with the lack of effect of scrambled peptides, provides strong evidence for the importance of C-terminal interactions. The interpretation that physical coupling is necessary (C64) is well-supported, though the authors appropriately note alternative mechanisms in the discussion.

result: SMLM-TIRF analysis in Pkd2fl/fl and Pkd2 ecKO cells confirms that PC-1 and PC-2 cluster properties are similar between Pkd1fl/fl and Pkd2fl/fl controls, and that PC-2 knockout similarly reduces both PC-1 and PC-2 surface clusters (to ~12.7% and 11.1% of control density), supporting bidirectional interdependency.
evaluation: Claims C138-C144 are supported by SMLM-TIRF imaging in Pkd2fl/fl and Pkd2 ecKO cells (Figure 5 supplements 3-4). The similar results in both knockout models (Pkd1 ecKO and Pkd2 ecKO) provide strong evidence for bidirectional interdependency. The consistency of cluster properties between Pkd1fl/fl and Pkd2fl/fl controls validates the approach. The interpretation of remaining fluorescence as nonspecific labeling is consistent across both knockout models.

result: Flow-mediated dilation inhibition in Pkd1/Pkd2 ecKO arteries is similar to that in single knockouts. Lowering bath Na+ inhibited flow-activated ICat in all genotypes. Combined with previous work, flow-mediated signaling and vasodilation are similarly attenuated in Pkd1 ecKO, Pkd2 ecKO, and Pkd1/Pkd2 ecKO mice.
evaluation: Claims C145-C147 are supported by comparison of myography data across genotypes and integration with prior work (MacKay et al., 2020). The similar magnitude of inhibition in double knockout compared to single knockouts provides strong evidence that PC-1 and PC-2 function in the same pathway rather than parallel pathways. The Na+ dependence (C146) supports the cation current mechanism.

result: Summary conclusion: Flow stimulates PC-1-dependent cation currents in endothelial cells that induce arterial hyperpolarization, vasodilation (via eNOS, IK, and SK channels over the entire functional shear stress range), and blood pressure reduction. PC-1 and PC-2 coassemble into interdependent plasma membrane clusters, and knockout of either abolishes surface expression of both proteins.
evaluation: Claims C65-C71 represent the main conclusions synthesized from all experimental results. These summary claims are well-supported by the convergent evidence from multiple experimental approaches (electrophysiology, myography, blood pressure measurements, biochemistry, and multiple imaging modalities). The interdependence model is strongly supported by the similar phenotypes in single and double knockouts and the SMLM-TIRF data showing loss of both proteins when either is knocked out.

result: Summary of specific functional effects: EC-specific knockout of either PC-1 or PC-2 similarly inhibits flow-mediated biphasic currents, Ca2+ influx-dependent cation currents, arterial hyperpolarization, vasodilation over a broad shear stress range, and vasodilation via eNOS, IK, and SK channel activation.
evaluation: Claims C148-C152 summarize the functional phenotypes across multiple experimental approaches. These are well-supported by the data presented in Figures 1-2 and 6, combined with prior work. The consistency of effects across different functional readouts strengthens the overall conclusion about PC-1/PC-2 interdependence in flow sensing.

result: PC-1 knockout elevates blood pressure (consistent with Pkd2 ecKO mice). PC-1 and PC-2 do not contribute to ACh-induced vasodilation, and myogenic tone, depolarization-induced constriction, and passive diameter are similar in all knockout and control arteries, indicating no generalized endothelial or smooth muscle dysfunction.
evaluation: Claims C153-C155 are supported by blood pressure measurements (Figure 3) and myography controls (Figure 2 and 6 supplements). The specificity of effects to flow-mediated responses (C154) and preservation of other vascular functions (C155) are important for ruling out non-specific effects. The consistency with prior Pkd2 ecKO results strengthens the conclusion.

result: Proposed signaling mechanism: Flow-activated PC-1/PC-2 stimulates eNOS, IK, and SK channels, producing arterial hyperpolarization that reduces CaV1.2 channel activity in smooth muscle cells, decreasing intracellular Ca2+ and causing vasodilation and blood pressure reduction. This mechanism may extend to other resistance-size arteries.
evaluation: Claims C156-C158 present the proposed mechanistic model based on the experimental data and cited literature. The model is well-supported by the data showing PC-1/PC-2-dependent activation of eNOS and K+ channels, arterial hyperpolarization, and vasodilation. The extension to other resistance arteries (C158) is appropriately presented as speculation requiring future investigation. The mechanism is consistent with established vascular physiology.

result: Flow-sensing occurs in the endothelial cell body (plasma membrane) rather than cilia. When both PC-1 and PC-2 are expressed, they readily traffic to the plasma membrane. Knockout of either PC-1 or PC-2 does not alter total protein levels of the other but prevents surface localization, leading to intracellular retention. Flow activates a heteromeric PC-1/PC-2 complex in the plasma membrane.
evaluation: Claims C99, C103-C106, and C114 are supported by patch-clamp data showing plasma membrane currents (C99, C114), Western blots showing no change in total protein levels (C104), and SMLM-TIRF imaging showing loss of surface clusters but not total protein (C105). The conclusion that flow activates a heteromeric complex (C106) is supported by the lack of change in cluster properties under flow and the similar functional effects of PC-1 and PC-2 knockout.

result: Background knowledge claims about PC-1 and PC-2 structure, expression, proposed functions, ADPKD, and vascular biology.
evaluation: Claims C72-C93 represent established knowledge from the literature, appropriately cited. These provide necessary context for the study. The citations appear appropriate and the knowledge claims are consistent with the field. These are background claims rather than novel findings.

result: Background knowledge about primary cilia, their role in flow sensing in different cell types, and prior conflicting findings about PC-1/PC-2 localization and function in cilia versus plasma membrane.
evaluation: Claims C94-C98, C100, C107-C113 represent established and conflicting knowledge from the literature about cilia and PC-1/PC-2 function. These are appropriately cited and provide important context for why the current study's findings (plasma membrane localization and function) are significant. The authors appropriately acknowledge the debate in the field.

result: Background knowledge about PC-1/PC-2 physical interactions, trafficking requirements, channel properties, and potential activation mechanisms.
evaluation: Claims C101-C102, C115-C118, C121-C124, and C126 represent established knowledge about PC-1/PC-2 interactions and properties from prior studies. These are appropriately cited and provide context for the current study's findings about coiled-coil interactions and channel function. The knowledge is relevant to interpreting the peptide interference experiments.

result: Clinical relevance: Hypertension occurs in >60% of ADPKD patients before kidney dysfunction (average onset 30-34 years). The study raises the possibility that hypertension and cardiovascular disease in ADPKD patients may involve altered PC-1/PC-2 function in endothelial cells. Human ADPKD patients show loss of NO release and reduced endothelium-dependent dilation during increased blood flow. Hypertension may be associated with dysfunctional PC-1/PC-2 signaling in ECs.
evaluation: Claims C128-C132 combine established clinical knowledge (C128, C130-C131, appropriately cited) with speculation about implications of the current findings (C129, C132). The speculation is reasonable given the data showing elevated blood pressure in EC-specific knockouts and the known vascular phenotypes in ADPKD patients. However, these remain hypotheses requiring future clinical investigation.

result: Speculative mechanistic interpretations: Flow may stimulate physical coupling of PC-1/PC-2 coiled-coils to activate current, or interference peptides may uncouple constitutively bound coiled-coils. PC-1/PC-2 channels in ECs may contain other TRP subunits. Other mechanosensitive proteins (Piezo1, GPR68) may stimulate PC-1/PC-2-dependent currents.
evaluation: Claims C119-C120, C125, and C127 represent speculative interpretations and hypotheses for future investigation. While the peptide data support a role for coiled-coil interactions (C119-C120), the exact mechanism remains unclear. The possibilities of other TRP subunits (C125) or upstream mechanosensors (C127) are reasonable hypotheses but lack direct experimental support in this study. These are appropriately presented as speculation in the discussion.

result: Technical details: p-eNOS (S1176) phosphorylation leads to activation. SMLM-TIRF localization precision was 29.6±0.6 nm (Alexa 488) and 24.6±0.7 nm (Alexa 647). PC-1 and PC-2 cluster sizes and intercentroid distances were exponentially distributed. Costes' randomization did not alter overlap in Pkd1 ecKO cells.
evaluation: Claims C133-C137 represent technical details and methodological validations. The eNOS phosphorylation knowledge (C133) is established and appropriately cited. The SMLM technical parameters (C134-C137) are well-documented in the methods and supplements. The localization precision is adequate for the measurements performed. The exponential distributions and randomization controls are appropriate statistical approaches.
